The King of Wú will be ashamed not to fight. He will certainly not wait for those who are yet to arrive, But will use the troops from the central states to fight us. If he boasts and comes after me, I will then trample his land. Those who arrive later will not be able to join the battle, I will use Yù'ér to oversee them. If the King of Wú becomes enraged and fights again, Bēn can then be sent out. If he does not fight but forms an alliance, The king can secure a good reputation and depart." The King of Yuè said: "Excellent!" He then thoroughly prepared the army, Preparing to attack Wú.
Chǔ Shēn Bāo Xū was sent as an envoy to Yuè. The King of Yuè, Gōu Jiàn, asked him, Saying: "The state of Wú acts contrary to the Way, They seek to destroy my state and ancestral temples, to turn them into flat land, and prevent them from receiving sacrifices. I wish to appeal to Heaven's justice against them, but though carriages, armor, soldiers, and military units are all prepared, May I ask, what is needed to make war possible?" Bāo Xū declined, saying, "I do not know." The king insisted on asking him, so he then replied, "Wú is indeed a strong state, capable of gaining extensive support from the various lords. May I ask what Your Majesty intends to use to fight them?" The king said, "Those who are by my side, with wine, sacrificial dishes, and simple meals, I have never dared not to share with them. I do not seek the best flavors in food, nor do I fully enjoy the sounds of music, seeking to repay Wú in this way. I wish to fight with this." Bāo Xū said, "Good is good, but it is not yet time to fight." The king said: "Within the state of Yuè, those who are sick, I inquire after them; those who die, I bury them; I care for their old, cherish their young, nurture their orphans, inquire about their illnesses, seeking to repay Wú. I wish to fight with this." Bāo Xū said: "Good is good, but it is not yet time to fight." The king said: "Within the state of Yuè, I treat the people leniently, regarding them as my children, treating them with loyalty and kindness. I revise laws and relax punishments, give the people what they want, remove what they hate, praise their good deeds, conceal their wrongdoings, seeking to repay Wú. I wish to fight with this." Bāo Xū said: "Good is good, "It is not yet possible to fight." The king said, "Within the state of Yuè, the wealthy, I will set them at ease; the poor, I will share with them; I will relieve their deficiencies and curtail their surpluses, so that both rich and poor benefit from it, seeking to repay Wú with this. I wish to fight with this." Bāo Xū said, "Good indeed, but it is not yet possible to fight." The king said, "Yuè borders Chǔ to the south, Jìn to the west, and Qí to the north. Each spring and autumn, with hides and silks, jade and silks, and daughters, we offer ourselves in submission, never daring to sever these ties, seeking to repay Wú with this. I wish to fight with this." Bāo Xū said, "Excellent, nothing could surpass it, yet still it is not possible to fight. For war, Wisdom is the beginning, benevolence is next, and courage is next. Without wisdom, one cannot know the ultimate condition of the people, and cannot assess the size of the multitudes under Heaven; without benevolence, one cannot share the hardships of hunger and toil with the army; without courage, one cannot resolve doubts and launch grand plans." The King of Yuè said: "Agreed."
The King of Yuè, Gōujiàn, then summoned the Five Great Officers, and said: "Wú is immoral, seeking to destroy our state altars and ancestral temples, turning them into plains, preventing offerings of blood and food. I wish to test the heart of Heaven with them. But although the chariots, armor, and soldiers are ready, I have no way to deploy them. I inquired of Wángsūn Bāoxū, and he has already given me his instructions. I dare to consult you, Great Officers, asking how to make the battle feasible. Gōu Jiàn wished for all the high officials to speak their minds, to all speak with sincerity, without flattery, for I intend to undertake great deeds." The high official Hòu Yōng then stepped forward and answered, "If rewards are judicious, then can we fight?" The king said, "Wise." The high official Kǔ Chéng stepped forward and answered, "If punishments are judicious, then can we fight?" The king said, "Fierce." The high official Zhǒng stepped forward and answered, "If resources are judicious, then can we fight?" The king said, "Discriminating." The high official Lí stepped forward and answered, "If preparations are judicious, then can we fight?" The king said, "Skillful." The high official Gāo Rú stepped forward and answered, "If sounds (of command) are judicious, then can we fight?" The king said, "Acceptable." The king then ordered the officials to issue a great decree throughout the state, saying: "All those who are in the military must report outside the gates of the capital." The king then gave orders to the state, saying: "Let those among the people who wish to report come forward. If you report that I, your ruler, am not wise and that I will bring misfortune and harm, within five days I will certainly investigate the matter. If more than five days pass, the right path will not be followed."
The King then went inside to instruct his wife (fū rén). The King stood with his back to the screen, the wife facing the screen. The King said: "From this day forward, no internal affairs shall go out, and no external affairs shall come in. If there is disgrace within, it is your responsibility; if there is disgrace without, it is my responsibility. I will see you here only." The King then went out. The wife saw the King off but did not go beyond the screen. She then closed the left door, filled it with earth, removed her hairpin, and sat to the side, not sweeping. The King stood with his back to the eaves, Dàfū Xiàng Yán. The king commanded Dàfū, saying: "The land tax is unevenly distributed, and the land is not well cultivated. Internally, this is a disgrace to the state; it is your fault. If the soldiers do not fight to the death, externally, there will be disgrace, and that is my fault. From this day forward, no internal affairs shall go out, and no external affairs shall come in. I shall see you only here and nowhere else." The king then departed. Dàfū saw the king off but did not go beyond the eaves. He then closed the left door, and filled it with earth, sitting to the side on a mat, without sweeping.
The king then went to the elevated platform, marched forward to the beat of drums, and arrived at the army. He executed those who were guilty and displayed them to the public, saying: "Let no one use gifts or jade ornaments to inquire about each other." The next day, they moved camp, and he executed those who were guilty and displayed them to the public, He said, "Let no one disobey the command to stay in their ranks like this." The next day, the camp was moved. A guilty person was executed and displayed to the troops, and he said, "Let no one disobey the king's command like this." The next day, the camp was moved, arriving at Yù'ér. A guilty person was executed and displayed to the troops, and he said, "Let no one be so licentious and unrestrained as to be unmanageable like this."
The king then ordered the officials to conduct a great muster in the army, saying, "If there are those whose parents are old and without brothers, report it." The king personally commanded them, saying, "I have a great matter, and you have old parents, but if you die for me, your parents will be left to tumble into ditches and ravines. Your service to me has already been significant. Return home and provide for your parents' remaining years. If there is a future matter, I will plan it with you." The next day, a muster was held in the army, and he said, "If there are brothers, four or five of you, all here, report it." The king personally gave the order, saying: "I have an important matter, you have brothers, four or five of you, all here. If the matter is unsuccessful, then it is all over. Choose one among you who wishes to return." The next day, he made an announcement throughout the army, saying: "If there are those who suffer from dizzy spells, report it." The king personally gave the order, saying: "I have an important matter. You suffer from dizzy spells, you should return if you wish. If there is anything in the future, I will discuss it with you." The next day, he made an announcement throughout the army, saying: "Those whose strength is insufficient to bear armor and weapons, whose will and conduct are insufficient to obey orders, may return, do not report it." The next day, he moved the army to Jiē Hé, executing the guilty as a warning, saying: "Let no one be like those whose will and conduct are indecisive." Thereupon, the people had the will to fight to the death. The King then ordered the officials to make a great proclamation throughout the army, saying: "Those who are told to return and do not return, to stay and do not stay, to advance and do not advance, to retreat and do not retreat, to go left and are not on the left, to go right and are not on the right, shall be beheaded, and their wives and children sold."
Thereupon, the King of Wú raised an army, and encamped north of the river. The King of Yuè encamped south of the river. The King of Yuè then divided his army in two, forming a left and right army, and used his personal troops, six thousand elite soldiers, as the central army. The next day, he prepared for a naval battle on the river. At dusk, he ordered the left army to hold their tongues, go five *lǐ* upstream and wait. He also ordered the right army to hold their tongues, cross the river five *lǐ* and wait. In the middle of the night, he ordered the left and right armies to cross the river, beat drums in mid-stream and wait. The Wú army heard this, and were greatly alarmed, saying: "The Yuè people have divided their army into two, They will use a pincer attack against our army." Thereupon, they did not wait for dawn, and also divided their army in half, intending to defend against Yuè. The King of Yuè then ordered his central army to cross in secret with bits in their mouths, without drums or shouting, to launch a surprise attack on them. The Wú army was greatly defeated. The left army and right army of Yuè then crossed over and followed them, and again greatly defeated them at Mò, and again defeated them in the suburbs. Three battles, three defeats, and then they reached Wú. The Yuè army then entered the state of Wú and surrounded the royal palace.
The King of Wú was afraid and sent someone to negotiate peace, saying: "In the past, I, the unworthy one, first entrusted control to the Lord of Yuè. You told me and asked for peace, men and women would obey. I could do nothing against the late Lord of Yuè, fearing Heaven's misfortune, not daring to cut off sacrifices, I granted you peace, and so it has continued until now. Now, I, the unworthy one, am without principle, Having offended the ruler, the ruler used his relatives to humiliate our humble state. I dare to ask for peace, and our men and women will serve as your servants." The King of Yuè said: "In the past, Heaven bestowed the state of Yuè upon Wú, but Wú did not accept it; today, Heaven bestows the state of Wú upon Yuè, how dare I not listen to the will of Heaven, and listen to your commands?" He then did not grant peace. Thereupon, he sent a man to inform the King of Wú, saying: "Heaven has bestowed the state of Wú upon Yuè, I dare not refuse to accept it. Because the lives of the people are not long, may Your Majesty not die! The people live on the earth, temporarily dwelling, how long will it be? I will relocate Your Majesty to Yǒngjù East, with three hundred couples, wherever Your Majesty finds peace, to pass away your years." Fūchā declined, saying: "Heaven has already sent calamity upon the state of Wú, not earlier or later, but on my very person, and I have indeed lost the ancestral temples and the altars of the state. In general, the lands and people of Wú are already possessed by Yuè. How can I, *gū* (I, the ruler), face the world?" As Fūchāi was about to die, he sent someone to say to Zǐ Xū: "If the dead are without knowledge, then it is over; but if they have knowledge, with what face shall I meet Yuán?" Thereupon, he committed suicide.
Yuè destroyed Wú and proceeded to conquer the superior states. The rulers of Sòng, Zhèng, Lǔ, Wèi, Chén, and Cài, holding their jade tokens, all came to court. It was precisely because he was able to humble himself before his ministers in order to gather their plans that he succeeded.
Yuè Yǔ 8.1 "Gōujiàn Destroys Wú"
King Gōujiàn of Yuè, residing on Mount Kuàijī, then issued an order to his three armies, saying: "All my fathers, elder brothers, younger brothers, and members of the royal family, if any can assist *guǎrén* (I, the lonely one) in devising a plan to repel Wú, I will share with him the administration of the state of Yuè." The grand master Zhǒng stepped forward and replied: "Your servant has heard that merchants stock up on furs in the summer and linen in the winter, boats in times of drought and carts in times of flooding, to prepare for scarcity. Even if there are no worries from all directions, it is essential to nurture and select strategists and capable officers . It is like seeking a raincoat and hat only when the seasonal rain arrives. One will surely seek them out. Now, the King, having already taken refuge on Mount Kuàijī, only then seeks strategists. Isn't that too late?" Gōujiàn said: "If I can but hear your words, Master, what lateness can there be?" He took his hand and consulted with him.
He then sent him to negotiate peace with Wú, saying: " My lord, Gōujiàn, having no one else to send, has sent his subject Zhǒng, daring not directly address the Heavenly King, but privately to the subordinate officials says: My lord's army is insufficient to disgrace you, wishing to offer gold, jade, The humiliation of sons and daughters bribing the ruler, I request that Gōujiàn's 句踐 daughter be given to the king as a concubine, the daughters of the grand officers be given to the grand officers as concubines, and the daughters of the knights be given to the knights as concubines. All the precious treasures of the Yuè 越 state will follow. Your humble servant will lead the multitude of the Yuè 越 state to follow your majesty's army, only at your majesty's command. If the sins of the Yuè 越 state are considered unforgivable, we will burn our ancestral temples, imprison our wives and children, sink gold and jade into the river, and have five thousand soldiers in armor who will fight to the death, and surely there will be an adversary. Thus, ten thousand armored men will serve your majesty. Would it not hurt what the king loves? Rather than kill these people, it would be better to gain this state. Which is more beneficial?"
Fūchāi 夫差 was about to agree to a settlement with them, Zǐxū 子胥 advised, "That is not acceptable. For the states of Wú 吳 and Yuè 越 are enemy states in a hostile war. They are surrounded by the three rivers, and the people have nowhere to move. If there is Wú 吳, there will be no Yuè 越; If there is Yuè, then there will be no Wú. This situation will be irreversible. Yuán has heard that, land people live on land, water people live on water. As for the state of Shàngdǎng, even if we attack and conquer it, we cannot live on its land, we cannot ride in their carriages. As for the state of Yuè, even if we attack and conquer it, we can live on its land, we can ride in their boats. This is its advantage, it cannot be lost, Your Majesty must destroy it. If this advantage is lost, even if you regret it, it will surely be too late."
The people of Yuè adorned eight beautiful women and presented them to Tài Zǎi Pǐ, saying: "If you can only pardon the crimes of the state of Yuè, there are even more beautiful women than these who will be presented." Tài Zǎi Pǐ advised, saying: "Pǐ has heard that those who attacked states in ancient times only sought their submission. Now they have already submitted, Yòu hé qiú yān." (What more is there to ask for?) Fūchāi yǔ zhī chéng ér qù zhī. (Fūchāi made peace with him and departed.)
Gōujiàn shuì yú guórén yuē: (Gōujiàn addressed the people of his state, saying:) "Guǎrén bùzhī qí lì zhī bùzú yě, (I, your ruler, was unaware of the insufficiency of my strength,) ér yòu yǔ dàguó zhí chóu, (and engaged in enmity with a powerful state,) yǐ bàolù bǎixìng zhī gǔ yú zhōngyuán, (thereby exposing the bones of the common people in the central plains.) Cǐ zé guǎrén zhī zuì yě. (This is my fault.) Guǎrén qǐng gēng." (I, your ruler, ask to change things.) Yúshì zàng sǐzhě, (Thereupon, he buried the dead,) wèn shāngzhě, (inquired after the wounded,) yǎng shēngzhě, (cared for the living,) diào yǒu yōu, (condoled with those who had sorrows,) hè yǒu xǐ, (congratulated those who had joys,) sòng wǎng zhě, (saw off those who were departing,) yíng lái zhě, (welcomed those who were arriving,) qù mín zhī suǒ è, (removed what the people hated,) bǔ mín zhī bùzú. (and supplemented what the people lacked.) Ránhòu bēi shì Fūchāi, (Then he humbly served Fūchāi,) huàn shì sānbǎi rén yú Wú, (sending three hundred officials as servants to Wú,) qí shēn qīn wèi Fūchāi qián mǎ. (and personally acted as Fūchāi's leading horse.)
Gōujiàn zhī dì, (Gōujiàn's territory,) nán zhì yú Gōuwú, (extended south to Gōuwú,) běi zhì yú Yùér, (north to Yùér,) dōng zhì yú Yín, (east to Yín,) xī zhì yú Gūmiè, (west to Gūmiè,) guǎng yùn bǎilǐ. (spanned a hundred *lǐ* in width.) Then he summoned his parents and brothers and swore to them, saying: "I have heard that the virtuous rulers of old had the people of the four directions flocking to them, like water flowing downwards. Now I am not capable of this; I will use you, my generals and officers, and your wives to increase the population." He ordered that strong men should not marry old women, and that old men should not marry strong wives. If a girl of seventeen is not married, her parents are guilty; if a man of twenty is not married, his parents are guilty. Those who are about to give birth must be reported, and the public doctor will attend to them. If a male child is born, two *hú* of wine and one dog are given; if a female child is born, two *hú* of wine and one pig are given. If three children are born, the state will provide a mother for them; if two children are born, the state will provide rations for them. When the head of a household dies, he shall be relieved of his duties for three years; when a branch family member dies, he shall be relieved of his duties for three months. He would certainly weep and bury them, as if they were his own sons. He would take into official service the orphaned sons, widows, those suffering from illness, and the poor and sick. He would take into official service their sons. As for accomplished men, he would ensure their dwellings were clean, their clothing beautiful, and their food plentiful, and he would urge them on with righteousness. Scholars coming from all directions, he would treat with the utmost respect. Gōujiàn would load rice and cooking oil onto boats to travel, and the children of the state playing, none were not fed, none were not given drink, and he would certainly ask their names. What was not grown by his own hand he would not eat, what was not woven by his own wife he would not wear. For ten years he did not take from the state, and the people all had three years' worth of food.
The elders of the state requested, saying: "Formerly, Fūchāi shamed our lord in the states of the nobles, now the state of Yuè is also frugal, please, let us avenge ourselves." Gōujiàn declined, saying: "In the past battle, it was not the fault of you gentlemen, but my fault. How could someone like me, dwelling in comfort, understand shame? Please, for now, let us not fight." The fathers and elder brothers again pleaded, saying: "Within the borders of the Yuè kingdom, our relationship with our ruler is like that of children to their parents. If a son thinks of avenging his parents' enemies, and a minister thinks of avenging his ruler's enemies, who would dare not exert all their strength? Please, let us fight again." Jù Jiàn, having granted their request, then gathered his troops and swore to them, saying: "I have heard that the wise rulers of old did not worry about the lack of numbers in their army, but worried about the lack of a sense of shame in their will and conduct. Now, Fū Chā has 130,000 men clad in water buffalo hide armor, and does not worry about the lack of a sense of shame in their will and conduct, but worries about the lack of numbers in his army. Now I will assist in the majesty of Heaven. I do not desire the bravery of a single man, but desire that they advance and retreat together. Those who advance should think of reward, those who retreat should think of punishment. If this is so, then there will be regular rewards. "To advance without risking one's life, and to retreat without shame, for such, there shall be the regular penalty." He indeed implemented this, and the people of the state all encouraged each other. Fathers exhorted their sons, elder brothers exhorted their younger brothers, wives exhorted their husbands, saying: "Who is our lord? And how can we avoid dying for him?" Therefore, they defeated Wú at Yòu, and again defeated them at Méi, and then defeated them in the suburbs.
Fūchāi sued for peace, saying: "This unworthy one's army is not sufficient to disgrace you. Allow me to use gold, jade, and women to atone for your disgrace." Gōujiàn replied, saying: "In the past, Heaven gave Wú to Yuè, but Wú did not accept the mandate; today, Heaven gives Wú to Yuè, how can Yuè not listen to Heaven's mandate and listen to your command! I will connect Wáng Yǒngjù in the east, and I will be two lords with you." Fūchā answered, "I have already performed the rituals before eating a meal. If you, my lord, do not forget the Zhōu dynasty, and consider the dilapidated state of my humble country, that is also my wish. If you were to say, 'I will destroy your altars of soil and grain, and exterminate your ancestral temples,' I would rather die. What face would I have to face the world!" The lord of Yuè took the next step, and consequently destroyed Wú.
8.2 *Fàn Lǐ's Advice to Gōujiàn on Maintaining Prosperity, Stabilizing Decline, and Regulating Affairs*
Three years after King Gōujiàn of Yuè ascended the throne, he desired to attack Wú. Fàn Lǐ advised him, saying, "In matters of state, there is maintaining prosperity, stabilizing decline, and regulating affairs." The king said, "What are the ways for these three?" He replied, "Maintaining prosperity is in accordance with Heaven, stabilizing decline is in accordance with Man, and regulating affairs is in accordance with Earth. The king did not ask, and Lí (蠡) dared not speak. The way of Heaven is full but does not overflow, flourishing but not arrogant, working hard but not boasting of its accomplishments. Now, the sage acts according to the times; this is called abiding by the times. When the time of Heaven is not right, do not become a guest of others; when human affairs have not arisen, do not be the one to initiate them. Now, you, my king, are not yet full but overflow, not yet flourishing but are arrogant, do not work hard but boast of your accomplishments, the time of Heaven is not right but you take the initiative to be a guest of others, human affairs have not arisen but you create and initiate them; this is contrary to Heaven and not harmonious with people. If the king does this, it will be detrimental to the country and bring ruin to your own person." The king did not listen.
Fàn Lǐ (范蠡) further admonished, saying: "Courage is contrary to virtue; weapons are ominous instruments; contention This is the end of the matter. Secret plots and actions against virtue, fondness for using deadly weapons, if these originate with a person, they will be the end of that person. Excessive indulgence in pleasure is forbidden by Shangdì, those who engage in this first will not prosper." The King said, "Let there be no more of such dissenting words, I have already made my decision!" Indeed, he raised an army and attacked Wú. They fought at Wǔ Hú, and were not victorious, retreating to Kuàijī to fortify themselves.
The King summoned Fàn Lǐ and asked him, saying, "I did not heed your words, and have come to this. What is to be done?" Fàn Lǐ replied, "Has the King forgotten it? To maintain fullness, one must act with Heaven; to stabilize what is toppling, one must act with people; to moderate affairs, one must act with Earth." The King said, "How should we deal with them?" He replied: "Use humble words and bestow respectful gifts, offer beautiful objects and female musicians, honor them with titles. If this is not enough, then you yourself should personally engage in trade with them." The King said: "Agreed." Thereupon, he ordered the grand master Dàfū Zhǒng 大夫種 to negotiate peace with Wú 吳, saying: "Request that commoners marry commoner women, and grand masters marry grand master women, and accompany them with the most important treasures of the state." The people of Wú 吳 did not agree. Dàfū Zhǒng 大夫種 came and returned again, saying: "We request to entrust the pipes and keys, and everything pertaining to the state, and personally accompany them, allowing your ruler to govern them." The people of Wú 吳 agreed. The King said: "Lí 蠡, remain to guard the state for me." He replied: "Within the borders, in matters concerning the people, Lí 蠡 is not as capable as Zhǒng 種. Outside the borders, the institutions of enemy states, matters requiring immediate decisions, Zhǒng is even inferior to Lí." The king said, "Agreed." He ordered the Grand Master Zhǒng to remain and guard the state, and accompanied Fàn Lǐ to enter officialdom in Wú.
After three years, the people of Wú dismissed them. Upon returning and arriving in the state, the king asked Fàn Lǐ, "What is the proper way to manage affairs?" He replied, "Managing affairs is like managing land. Only land can encompass all things and unify them as one, so that affairs are not neglected. It produces all things, and shelters birds and beasts, then receives their names and benefits from them all. Good and bad both come to fruition to nourish life. When the time is not ripe, one cannot force growth; when a matter is not fully investigated, one cannot force completion. By remaining as such, Use it to measure the world, await those who come and correct them, determine it according to what is appropriate for the time. Equalize the labor of men and women, eliminate the harm to the people, in order to avoid heavenly disasters. The fields are opened up, the granaries are full, and the people are prosperous. Do not leave its people idle, so as to become a ladder to chaos. When the times are about to revolt, and affairs are about to have leisure, one must know the constant rules of heaven and earth, then one can have the successful benefit of the world. If affairs have no leisure, and times have no revolt, then soothe the people and protect teaching to await them."
The king said: "This state of mine, is the state of Lí (蠡), Lí (蠡), plan it!" He replied: "Within the borders, the affairs of the common people, the festivals and three joys, not disrupting the people's work, Do not go against the seasons; May the five grains ripen in harmony; Then the people will multiply and flourish; May the ruler and ministers, both above and below, each attain their aspirations; The clam is not as good as planting crops. Beyond the four borders, Dealing with enemy states, Making decisive judgments, Rely on the constancy of yin and yang, Follow the regularity of Heaven and Earth, Be flexible but not yielding, Be strong but not rigid, The practice of virtue and severity, Should be used as the norm; Life and death follow the punishments of Heaven and Earth, Heaven relies on man, The sage relies on Heaven; Man brings himself into being, Heaven and Earth give him form, The sage then completes him. Therefore, win battles but do not seek revenge, Take land but do not return it, Military victories are achieved abroad, Good fortune arises within, Exert little effort yet have a bright and illustrious reputation, Planting is still not as good as the clam." The king said: "Yes." He ordered Grand Master Zhǒng to do it.
8.3 "Fàn Lǐ Advises Gōu Jiàn Not to Prematurely Plan Against Wú"
In the fourth year, the king summoned Fàn Lǐ and asked him, saying: "My predecessor passed away, and I, the unworthy one, ascended the throne. I am still young, and have not yet developed a constant way, When I go out, I am wild about hunting, When I return, I am wild about wine. My people are not in my plans, only boats and carriages are. Heaven has sent disaster upon Yuè, entrusting control to Wú. The people of Wú are even more oppressive towards me, indeed, it is even worse. I wish to discuss this with you, is it possible?" He replied, "It is not yet possible. I, Lǐ, have heard that, If Heaven does not approve, adhering to the opposite of the opportune time, forcefully demanding brings misfortune. If one does not succeed when the time is right, Will instead receive its calamity. Loss of virtue and destruction of name, wandering and death. There is seizing, there is giving, there is not giving, the king did not plan early. Oh, Wú, it is the king's Wú, if the king had planned it early, the matter would still be unknowable." The king said: "Yes."
8.4 *Fàn Lǐ Says Human Affairs Have Arrived But Heaven's Response Has Not Yet Arrived*
Another year, the king summoned Fàn Lǐ and asked him, saying: "I and you planned against Wú, you said 'it is not yet permissible'. Now the King of Wú indulges in pleasure and forgets his people, disrupts the people's labor, goes against the seasons; trusts slander, delights in actors, hates helpers and distances advisors, the sage does not emerge, "Loyal ministers dissect their bones [to offer advice]; all crookedly accommodate each other; none dares to criticize each other; superiors and inferiors deceive each other. Is this acceptable?" He replied, "Human affairs have reached their limit, but the heavenly response has not yet come. Your Majesty, please wait for it." The king said, "Agreed."
8.5 *Fàn Lǐ Said That To Presage an Event Before Its Time Leads to Failure*
Another year passed, the king summoned Fàn Lǐ and asked him, saying, "I discussed attacking Wú with you, and you said, 'It is not yet possible.' Now Shēn Xū repeatedly remonstrated with his king, and the king became angry and killed him. Is it now possible?" He replied, "Defiant behavior is budding. Before Heaven and Earth have taken shape, to presage an event before its time causes the matter to fail [Zá] They all received the punishment. [Wáng gū] The king should wait for it." The king said: "Agreed."
8.6 *Fàn Lǐ Wèi Rénshì Yǔ Tiāndì Xiāngcān Nǎi Kěyǐ Chénggōng* (Fàn Lǐ said that human affairs must be combined with the principles of heaven and earth in order to succeed)
After another year, the king summoned Fàn Lǐ and asked him, saying: "I discussed attacking Wú with you, and you said 'It is not yet possible.' Now their rice and crabs are not spared even a seed, is it possible now?" He replied: "The heavenly signs should be at their peak, but human efforts are not yet exhausted. The king should wait for it." The king angrily said: "Is this principle fixed, or are you deceiving me with nonsense? I am discussing human affairs with you, and you respond to me with heavenly timing; now the heavenly signs should be at their peak, and you respond to me with human affairs. What is the reason for this?" Fàn Lǐ replied: "Wáng Gū, please do not be offended. The affairs of a ruler must be in accordance with Heaven and Earth, only then can they be successful. Now, the disaster is new, and the people are fearful. Their ruler and ministers, both high and low, all know that their resources are insufficient to sustain a long period. They will unite their strength, devote their lives, and even then, victory is uncertain. Your Majesty, you should still engage in hunting, but not to the point of neglecting your duties; the pleasures of the palace, not to the point of excessive drinking; indulge in banquets and drinks with the ministers, but do not forget the norms of the state. If their superiors treat them with little virtue, the people will exhaust their strength, and if they are made to hope for food but cannot obtain it, then you can bring about the punishment of Heaven and Earth. Your Majesty, please wait for it."
8.7 "Yuè Raises Troops to Attack Wú but Does Not Engage in Battle"
When it came to the eleventh month, the King summoned Fàn Lǐ and asked him, saying: "There is a saying: 'A large drink cannot compare to a pot of cooked rice.' "The year is now late, what are you going to do?" He replied: "If not for your words, my lord, I was just about to request an audience with you. I have heard that those who follow the times are like putting out a fire or chasing a fugitive. They must stumble and rush forward, fearing only that they will not reach in time." The king said: "Agreed." Thereupon, he raised an army to attack Wú, reaching the Five Lakes.
The people of Wú heard of this and came out to challenge them, five times in one day. The king could not bear it and wanted to agree to battle. Fàn Lǐ stepped forward to advise: "If a plan made in the halls of the court is lost in the central plains, Cáo Guì asked Duke Zhuāng about the reasons for fighting. The Duke said: "I do not begrudge clothing and food to the people, nor do I begrudge sacrificial animals and jade to the gods." Cáo Guì replied: "It is only when kindness is rooted that the people will return with their loyalty; it is only when the people are harmonious that the gods will send down blessings. If you spread virtue among the people and make your governance fair, gentlemen will devote themselves to governing, and commoners will devote themselves to their labor; actions will not violate the proper time, and wealth will not exceed what is needed; if wealth and resources are not depleted, there will be none who cannot be made to participate in communal sacrifices. Therefore, when employing the people, none will disobey; when seeking blessings, none will be lacking. Now, you are about to bestow kindness with small gifts, and offer sacrifices with exclusive reverence. Small gifts are not universal, and exclusive reverence is not generous. If not universal, the people will not return; if not generous, the gods will not bless you. What will you use to fight? The people seek to be not deficient in wealth, and the gods seek to be richly provided with offerings; therefore, you cannot but attend to the fundamentals." The Duke said, "When I hear lawsuits, though I may not be able to discern (the truth), I will surely decide them with fairness." He replied, "That is acceptable. If you truly have the people at heart, even if your wisdom is not sufficient, you will surely attain it."
2.2 "Cáo Guì Advises Duke Zhuāng Against Going to Qí to Observe the Community Altar Festival"
Duke Zhuāng went to Qí to observe the community altar festival. Cáo Guì remonstrated, saying, "You must not. Ritual, is what is used to regulate the people. Therefore, the former kings established the feudal lords, causing them to pay court four times every five years, and to have one chief minister pay court once. At the end, they would discuss matters in assemblies, in order to correct the meanings of ranks and titles, to guide the order of seniority, to instruct in the rules of superiors and inferiors, and to regulate the economy of resources. There is no reason for negligence in between. Now, if Qí abandons the laws of Tàigōng and observes the people at the community altar, and the ruler initiates this practice and goes to observe it, it is not an established practice. How will you instruct the people? Establishing a community altar in the earth assists with the seasons. Collecting the gleanings and offering them up is incorporating the essentials. Now, Qí establishes a community altar and goes to observe the multitude, which is not the instruction of the former kings. The Son of Heaven sacrifices to the Supreme God, and the feudal lords attend to receive mandates there. The feudal lords sacrifice to their former kings and former dukes, and the high ministers assist them in receiving tasks. Your servant has not heard of feudal lords gathering to sacrifice together, and the sacrifice is not in accordance with the law. Every action of the ruler must be recorded, and if the record is not in accordance with the law, what will future generations observe?" The Duke did not listen, and went to Qí.
2.3 "Artisan Qìng Advises Duke Zhuāng Against Red Pillars and Carved Rafters"
Duke Zhuāng had the pillars of the Huán palace painted red and its rafters carved. The artisan Qìng said to the Duke: "Your servant has heard that the ancestors of the sagely kings and dukes, when establishing their fiefs, left behind laws for their descendants, so that they would not fall into evil. They did so to make the good reputation of their predecessors shine upon later generations, making it a constant guide in the world, thereby enabling them to maintain a firm and lasting hold, enduring for a long time. Now, the late lord was frugal, while you, my lord, are extravagant. This diminishes the good virtue." The Duke said, "I intend to embellish it." He replied, "It will not benefit you, my lord, but will diminish the good virtue of your predecessor. Therefore, your servant says it would be best to stop." The Duke did not listen.
2.4 Xiàfǔ Zhǎn Advises on Zōngfù Dí (Meeting) with Āi Jiāng Using Gifts
When Āi Jiāng arrived, the Duke sent a senior official and the women of the clan to meet her with gifts. Xiàfǔ Zhǎn of the clan said, "This is not according to custom." The Duke said, "The ruler establishes the custom." He replied, "If the ruler establishes a custom that is in accordance, then it becomes the custom. If they act rebelliously, then it should also be recorded as their rebellion. As a subordinate official, I fear that their rebellion will be recorded for posterity, therefore I dare not fail to report it. The gifts exchanged between husband and wife should not exceed jujubes and chestnuts, in order to show reverence. For men, jade, silk, fowl, and birds are used to distinguish the different objects. Now the woman holds the gifts, this is a lack of distinction between men and women. The distinction between men and women is a major principle of the state, and cannot be absent." The Duke did not listen.
2.5 *Zāng Wénzhòng Rú Qí Gào Dí*
Lǔ was experiencing famine. Zāng Wénzhòng spoke to Duke Zhuāng, saying: "To act as assistance to the four neighboring states, to strengthen trust among the feudal lords, to emphasize this with marriage alliances, to reinforce it with sworn covenants, is done for the purpose of securing the state's difficulties and emergencies. To cast famous ritual vessels, to store precious wealth, is done to await the suffering of the people from diseases. "Now the state is sick, why doesn't Your Lordship use titles and regalia to request grain from Qí!" The Duke said, "Who should I send?" He replied, "When the state suffers famine, ministers go out to request grain, this is the ancient system. Chén is prepared to be a minister, Chén requests to go to Qí." The Duke sent him.
A follower said, "The lord did not order you, you requested it yourself, is this choosing duties?" Wén Zhòng said, "The worthy are eager to relieve suffering and yield to the ordinary, those in office should manage affairs and not avoid difficulties, those in high positions should be concerned about the people's suffering, therefore the state has no troubles. Now our situation is not as dire as Qí's, it is not an emergency. Those above do not care for those below, those in office are lazy, this is not serving the lord."
Wén Zhòng went to Qí with fragrant wine in a black jade ceremonial vessel (chàng guī) and a jade chime stone (yù qìng) to request grain, He said: "Natural disasters are rampant, descending upon our humble city, famines repeatedly strike, the people are weak and near death, we greatly fear the lack of offerings to Zhōu Gōng and Tài Gōng, and the consequent failure to provide regular tribute and service, incurring punishment. With humble offerings, the ceremonial vessels of our late ruler, we dare to report our financial difficulties, in order to ease your burdens; to rescue our impoverished city, enabling us to fulfill our duties. Surely not only our ruler and a few ministers will receive your gracious gifts, but Zhōu Gōng, and Tài Gōng, along with all the gods and spirits, will eternally enjoy and rely upon them!" The people of Qí returned their jade and gave them grain for purchase.
2.6 *Zhǎn Qín Sends Yǐ Xǐ to Console the Army with Ointment*
Qí Xiào Gōng came to attack Lǔ. Zāng Wénzhòng wanted to use diplomatic words to inform them, but he was worried about it, and asked Zhǎn Qín. He replied: "I have heard that, when dealing with a great power, one teaches with humility, and when dealing with a small matter, one serves the great power, Therefore, to ward off chaos, it's useless to rely on words. If a small state acts arrogantly and provokes a large state, causing it to inflict chaos upon itself, with chaos already at hand, what good are words then?" Wén Zhòng 文仲 said, "The state is in dire straits! When facing emergency, everything is employed if it can be, and there will be no hesitation in utilizing it. I wish to use your words as gifts to appease them; is that acceptable?"
Zhǎn Qín 展禽 sent Yǐ Xǐ 乙喜 with ointments and perfumes to犒(kào)lào the army, saying, "Our ruler is inept and unable to serve those who guard the borders, causing Your Excellency to be greatly angered, and to be exposed in the fields of our dilapidated state. I dare to犒(kào)lào your esteemed army." The Duke of Qí 齊侯 saw the envoy and said, "Is the state of Lǔ 魯國 afraid?" The envoy replied, "The petty people are afraid, but the gentlemen are not." The Duke said, "The house is like an empty bell, and the fields have no green grass. What do you rely on that you are not afraid?" He replied: "I rely on what the two former rulers were entrusted to do. In the past, King Chéng ordered my former ruler, the Duke of Zhōu, and the former ruler of Qí, the Grand Duke, saying: 'You are the arms and legs of the Zhōu house, to assist the former kings. I grant you land, secured with sacrifices, so that generations of descendants will not harm each other.' Now, you, Lord, have come to punish the crimes of my humble city, it should also be to make us listen and then release us, and will surely not destroy our state. How could they be greedy for land and abandon the mandate of the former kings? How then would they pacify the lords? I rely on this to not be afraid." The Marquis of Qí then agreed to make peace and returned.
2.7 Zāng Wénzhòng Persuades Duke Xī to Request the Release of Duke Chéng of Wèi
At the meeting in Wēn, the people of Jìn arrested Duke Chéng of Wèi and returned him to Zhōu, and had a doctor poison him. He did not die, and the doctor was not punished either.
Zāng Wénzhòng said to Duke Xī: "That Lord of Wèi is probably without guilt. There are only five types of punishments, none of which are concealed; concealment is avoidance. Therefore, the great are displayed in the open fields, the small are carried out in the marketplace, the five punishments are applied three times, thus there is no concealment. Now, the people of Jìn poisoned the Marquis of Wèi, but he did not die, and yet they do not punish their envoy; they avoid and resent killing him. If there is a request from the feudal lords, he will surely be spared. I have heard it said: Distributing fairly brings concern for one another, therefore, there can be affection. The troubles of the feudal lords, the feudal lords should be concerned for them, this is how to instruct the people. Why doesn't Your Lordship request the release of the ruler of Wèi to show affection to the feudal lords, and also to influence Jìn? Jìn has newly acquired feudal lords, and they will also say: "If Lǔ does not abandon its relatives, then it cannot be treated with disdain." The Duke was pleased, and presented twenty jué of jade, and thus the Marquis of Wèi was released.
From this point onward, Jìn's embassies to Lǔ were elevated one grade above those to other feudal lords, with equal rank, and increased emphasis on gifts and goods. The Marquis of Wèi, hearing that this was due to Zāng Wénzhòng, sent him bribes. He declined, saying: "The words of an external minister do not cross borders, I dare not involve myself with the ruler."
2.8 "Zāng Wénzhòng Requests Reward for the Important Lodging Official"
Duke Wén of Jìn distributed territory seized from Cáo to the feudal lords. Duke Xī sent Zāng Wénzhòng to go, and he stayed at the Important Lodging. The Important Lodging official told him: "Jìn is beginning to establish hegemony and desires to secure the feudal lords, therefore it distributes the territory of the guilty to the feudal lords. None of the feudal lords fail to hope for a share and desire to be close to Jìn, and they will all compete to be first. If Jìn does not firmly establish a ranking, it will surely favor those who are first. My son, you must hasten your departure. If Lǔ is at the forefront and ahead of others, what will the other lords look to? If you delay even a little, I fear it will be too late." He followed this advice and acquired much territory from the other lords. Upon returning, having reported back, he requested on his behalf, saying: "The abundance of land is due to the efforts of the gatekeeper. I have heard it said: 'If good deeds are evident, even a small reward is appropriate; if evil deeds have origins, even a great punishment is warranted.' Now, with a single word, he has expanded our borders, his deed is greatly evident, I request that he be rewarded." Thereupon, he was brought forth and ennobled.
2.9 Zhǎn Qín Discusses the Inappropriateness of Sacrificing to Yuán Jū as a Matter of Governance.
A seabird called "Yuán Jū" stopped outside the east gate of Lǔ for three days, and Zāng Wénzhòng ordered the people of the state to sacrifice to it. Zhǎn Qín said: "How excessive, "How excessive is Zāngsūn's 臧孫 administration! Ritual sacrifices are a major principle of the state, and these principles are what constitute good governance. Therefore, careful regulation of sacrifices establishes the norms of the state. Now, to increase these norms without reason is inappropriate for good governance.
"The system of sacrifices established by the sage kings was such that those who benefited the people through their laws were sacrificed to; those who diligently served their duties unto death were sacrificed to; those who stabilized the state through their labor were sacrificed to; those who could ward off great disasters were sacrificed to; and those who could defend against great calamities were sacrificed to. Those who did not belong to these categories were not included in the sacrificial canon. In the past, when the Lièshān 烈山 Clan possessed the world, their son was named Zhù 柱, who was able to cultivate all kinds of grains and vegetables; and with the rise of the Xià 夏 dynasty, Zhōu Qì 周棄 succeeded him, so he was sacrificed to as Jì 稷 (god of millet). When Gònggōng 共工 Clan dominated the nine provinces, their son was named Hòutǔ 后土, who was able to pacify the nine lands, so he was sacrificed to as Shè 社 (god of the soil). Huángdì was able to establish names for all things, in order to enlighten the people and equitably distribute wealth; Zhuānxū was able to continue this. Dì Kù was able to regulate the three celestial markers to secure the people; Yáo was able to simplify and equalize penal laws to provide standards for the people; Shùn diligently attended to the people's affairs and died in the wilderness; Gǔn blocked the floodwaters and was executed; Yǔ was able to cultivate virtue to complete Gǔn's work; Xiè served as Minister of Education, and the people were harmonious; Míng diligently performed his office and died in the water; Tāng governed the people with leniency and eliminated their wickedness; Jì diligently cultivated the hundred grains and died in the mountains; King Wén manifested virtue through culture, King Wǔ removed the filth from the people. Therefore, the Yǒuyú氏 clan performed the *dì* sacrifice to Huángdì and took Zhuānxū as their ancestor, offered suburban sacrifices to Yáo and venerated Shùn as their progenitor; The Xiàhòu氏 clan performed the *dì* sacrifice to Huángdì and took Zhuānxū as their ancestor, offered suburban sacrifices to Gǔn and venerated Yǔ as their progenitor; The Shāng people performed the *dì* sacrifice to Shùn and took Xiè as their ancestor, offered suburban sacrifices to Míng and venerated Tāng as their progenitor; The Zhōu people performed the *dì* sacrifice to Dì Kù and offered suburban sacrifices to Jì, took King Wén as their ancestor and venerated King Wǔ as their progenitor. Mù, was one who could lead Zhuānxū, the Yǒuyú氏 clan honored him; Zhù, was one who could lead Yǔ, the Xiàhòu氏 clan honored him; Shàngjiǎ Wēi, was one who could lead Xiè, The Shang people offer sacrifices to them; Gāo Yǔ, Dà Wáng, they were able to lead Jì, the Zhou people offer sacrifices to them. Generally, the *dì* sacrifice, the suburban sacrifice, the ancestral sacrifice, the lineage sacrifice, and the requital sacrifice, these five are the state's canonical sacrifices.
"Adding to these the gods of soil and grain, mountains and rivers, all of whom have meritorious achievements towards the people; as well as former wise and virtuous people, who serve as clear examples; and the three luminaries of the heavens, which the people look up to; and the five elements of the earth, which are responsible for growth and reproduction; and the famous mountains, rivers, and marshes of the nine provinces, which produce resources and utilities. If they are not of these categories, they are not within the sacrificial canon.
"Now, the sea bird has arrived, yet you already sacrifice to it without understanding, considering it a state canon, it is difficult to be considered benevolent and wise. The benevolent value merit, And a wise person deals with things. To sacrifice to someone without merit, is not benevolent; not to know and yet not to ask, is not wise. Is the sea going to have a disaster this year? The birds and beasts of the broad river, invariably know how to avoid their disasters."
That year, there were many strong winds at sea, and the winter was warm. Wén Zhòng heard the words of Liǔxià Jì, and said: "Truly, it is my fault, the words of Master Jì cannot but be followed." He had them written down as three precepts.
2.10 "Duke Wén wanted to demolish the houses of Mèng Wénzǐ and Kuài Jìngzǐ"
Duke Wén wanted to demolish the house of Mèng Wénzǐ, and sent someone to tell him, saying: "I want to benefit you with something broader externally." He replied: "Position, is the foundation of governance; offices are the markers of position; carriages and clothing The *biǎo* (表) is the symbol of merit. The *zhái* (宅, residence) comes next to the *zhāng* (章, symbol of merit). The *lù* (祿, emolument) is the food that comes next to the *cì* (次, residence). The ruler deliberates on these five matters to establish governance, seeking unchanging principles. Now, the officials came with an order to change your servant's office and his carriages and robes, and said: "We will change your residence for the sake of ease and benefit." Now, the office, is the place to revere the ruler's commands morning and night. Your servant has stood in the office of his late ancestors, and wears their carriages and robes. To change residence for the sake of benefit, is to disgrace the ruler's commands. I dare not accept the order. If I am guilty, then I request to return the emolument and carriages and robes and leave the office, and only take a residence assigned by the villagers." The Duke did not accept it. Zāng Wénzhòng (臧文仲) heard of it and said: "Mèng Sūn (孟孫) is good at preserving the past, he can indeed surpass Mù Bó (穆伯) and preserve his legacy in Lǔ (魯)!"
The Duke wanted to dismantle the residence of Xì Jìngzǐ (郤敬子), and the same issue arose. He replied: "My late ancestor Huì Bó (惠伯) was entrusted with the affairs of the *Sī Lǐ* (司里, a district), The number of times the ruler bestows blessed meat (君胙, jūn zuò) during the *cháng* (嘗, autumn sacrifice), *dì* (禘, grand sacrifice), *zhēng* (蒸, winter sacrifice), and *xiǎng* (享, regular sacrifice) ceremonies is fixed. The number of gifts presented when entering and exiting to receive instructions, carrying the ruler's orders, is also fixed. Now you order me to change my position in the outer court, treating me as an official who distributes orders by rank. Isn't this a violation of the rules? I request to follow the Minister of Instruction (司徒, Sītú) to change my position by rank." The Duke also did not accept this.
2.11 *Xiàfǔ Fújì Changes the Constant Order of Zhaomu*
*Xiàfǔ Fújì* was in charge of the ancestral temple (宗, zōng). He was about to elevate Duke *Xī* (僖公, Xī Gōng) in the *zhēng* sacrifice. The officials in charge of the ancestral temple said, "This is not in accordance with the *zhaomu* order." *Xiàfǔ* said, "I am the Minister of the Ancestral Temple (宗伯, Zōngbó). The one who is more prominent is *zhāo* (昭), and the next is *mù* (穆). What fixed rule is there?" The officials said, "The *zhaomu* order in the ancestral temple is based on the seniority of generations and the closeness or distance of kinship among descendants. Sacrificing demonstrates filial piety (孝, xiào), and everyone presents utmost reverence to their great ancestors, It is the ultimate in conspicuous filial piety. Therefore, the palace historians recorded the generations, and the temple scribes recorded the order of ancestral tablets (zhāo and mù), still fearing that they might overstep the boundaries. Now, to venerate the enlightened before the ancestors, from Xuán Wáng to Zhǔ Guǐ, none were superior to Tāng; from Jì to Wáng Jì, none were superior to Wén and Wǔ. In the seasonal sacrifices of Shāng and Zhōu, they never elevated Tāng alongside Wén and Wǔ, so as not to overstep the boundaries. Lǔ is not equal to Shāng and Zhōu, yet changes their established custom; is this not impermissible?" He was not listened to, and thus he elevated them.
Zhǎn Qín said: "Xiàfù Fú Jì will surely suffer calamity. The words of the temple officials are in accordance with tradition, and Xī has not made them clear. To offend tradition is inauspicious; to instruct the people with disorder is also inauspicious; to alter the ranks of the spirits is also inauspicious; to elevate them without understanding is also inauspicious; to offend the way of ghosts in two respects, to offend the way of men in two respects, how can there be no calamity?" The attendant said: "If there is misfortune, where does it lie? Is it in punishment and execution, or in premature death?" He said: "It is not yet knowable. If his blood and vital energy are strong and firm, he will likely reach the end of his life with favor. Even if he dies at an old age, it is not as if there is no misfortune." After a time, at his burial, the body was burned, and the smoke reached upward.
2.12 "Lǐ Gé Changes the Letter to Expel the Servant of the Crown Prince of Jǔ"
The servant of the Crown Prince of Jǔ assassinated Duke Jǐ, and came fleeing with his treasures. Duke Xuān sent a servant with a letter instructing Jì Wénzǐ, saying: "The Crown Prince of Jǔ did not hesitate to kill his lord for my sake, and came with his treasures, he loves me greatly. Give him a city for me. You must bestow it today, do not defy my order." Lǐ Gé encountered him and changed the letter, saying: "The Crown Prince of Jǔ killed his lord and stole his treasures to come here, not knowing to seek strength from what is distant but instead seeks it from what is nearby. Banish him to the barbarian lands for me. Today it must be passable, there will be no disobedience." The next day, the officials reported back. The Duke questioned them. The servant, Lǐ Gé, responded. The Duke seized him, and said: "He who disobeys the ruler's command, have you also heard of this?" He replied, "Your servant risked death to write, how could I not have heard of it! Your servant has heard it said: 'He who destroys the rules is a thief, he who hides a thief is a concealer, he who steals treasure is a traitor, he who uses the traitor's wealth is an adulterer.' To make the ruler a concealer of adulterers is not something that can be ignored. Your servant's disobedience to the ruler's command is also something that cannot go unpunished." The Duke said, "I am indeed greedy, it is not your fault." And so he released him.
2.13 *Pú Lǐ Gé* cuts and discards Duke *Xuān*'s nets
Duke Xuān excessively fished in the Sì River during the summer. Lǐ Gé cut his nets and threw them away, saying: "In ancient times, when the great cold descended and the earthworms emerged from hibernation, the water official (shuǐ yú) would then inspect the nets and weirs, catching named fish, and offering birds from the river, and tasting them in the ancestral temple, and distributing them throughout the state, to help disseminate the (seasonal) qi. When birds and beasts are pregnant, and aquatic insects develop, the beast official (shòu yú) would then prohibit the use of nets and traps, and preserve fish, turtles, and soft-shelled turtles to provision the summer, to help with growth and abundance. When birds and beasts are mature, and aquatic insects are pregnant, the water official (shuǐ yú) would then prohibit the use of seine nets, and set up pitfalls and snares, to fill the temple kitchen, and accumulate resources for use. Furthermore, trees on mountains should not have their shoots and suckers cut off, reeds in swamps should not be prematurely felled, young kūn and ér fish should be protected, young ní and mí deer should be allowed to grow, birds' wings should be allowed to develop, and eggs should be hatched, "Nourishing insects and fostering larvae, is to cultivate and multiply all things, this is an ancient teaching. Now, when fish are just beginning to spawn, without teaching them to grow, you also implement nets, a greed without limit."
The duke heard this and said: "I erred, and Lǐ Gé corrected me, is this not good! This is a good net indeed, for me to obtain the law. Have the officials store it away, so that I will not forget to reflect." Shī Cún attended, and said: "Storing the net is not as good as placing Lǐ Gé at your side, so you will not forget."
2.14 "Zǐ Shū Shēng Bó Declines a Town"
Zǐ Shū Shēng Bó went to Jìn to thank Jì Wén Zǐ, Xì Chōu wanted to give him a town, but he did not accept it. Upon returning, Bào Guó said to him: "Why did you decline the town of Kǔ Chéng Shū, were you trying to show sincere humility, or did you know it was impossible?" He replied, "I have heard it said, 'If one does not make the ridgepole thick, it cannot bear heavy weight.' Nothing is heavier than a state, and nothing is like virtue in a ridgepole. Now, Kǔchéng Shū's family desires to bear the weight of two states but lacks great virtue, it will surely not survive. Ruin will not be far off. It is like a disease, I fear it will easily spread. The Kǔchéng clan has three causes for ruin: little virtue but much favor, low rank but a desire to control the government, no great accomplishment but a desire for great reward; these are all storehouses of resentment. Their lord is arrogant and selfish. Upon returning victorious from battle, he will surely establish a new family. To establish a new family, without relying on the people, he cannot get rid of the old; to rely on the people, if there are not many resentful people, there is no starting point. To create three storehouses of resentment can be considered too many. If he cannot secure his own position, how can he give a city to someone else!'" Bào Guó said, "My trust is not as great as yours. If the Bào shì (鮑氏) clan has a feud, I will not scheme against you. Now, you plan for the distant future by yielding the city, you will certainly be permanently established."
2.15 *Lǐ Gé* (里革) Discusses the Ruler's Faults
The people of Jìn (晉) killed Duke Lì (厲公). A border guard informed Duke Chéng (成公), who was at court. The duke said, "The minister killed his ruler, whose fault is it?" None of the officials answered. *Lǐ Gé* (里革) said, "It is the ruler's fault. A ruler, his authority is great. To lose authority to the point of being killed, his faults are many. Moreover, a ruler is one who leads the people and corrects their wickedness. If the ruler indulges selfish deviations and abandons the affairs of the people, and the people nearby harbor evil, with no way to examine it, the wickedness will increase. If he uses wickedness to govern the people, To fall into decline without recovery; to employ good men but be unwilling to trust them completely; then they cannot be employed; to the point of utter destruction and none care for it. What use is it? Jié fled to Náncháo, Zhòu fell at Jīng, Lì was exiled to Zhì, Yōu perished at Xī, all these are examples of this principle. Now, a ruler is the rivers and lakes of the people. They act, and the people follow them. Whether good or bad, it's all due to the ruler. What can the people do?"
2.16 *Jì Wénzǐ's Discourse on Concubine and Horse*
Jì Wénzǐ, in his service to Xuān and Chéng, did not have concubines dressed in silk nor horses fed with grain. Zhòngsūn Tuō remonstrated, saying: "You are the highest minister of Lǔ, serving two rulers already. Your concubines not wearing silk, your horses not eating grain, people will consider you stingy, and also, will this not be unadorned for the state?" Wénzǐ said: "I also desire it. However, observing the people of the state, there are still many whose fathers and elder brothers eat coarse food and wear poor clothing. It is for this reason that I dare not. If the fathers and elder brothers of the people eat coarse food and wear poor clothing, while I have beautiful concubines and horses, would this not be failing to care for the people? Furthermore, I have heard that using virtue as glory is the splendor of a state, not using concubines and horses."
Wénzǐ told Mèng Xiànzǐ about this, and Xiànzǐ imprisoned him for seven days. From then on, Zǐfú's concubines' clothing did not exceed seven shēng of cloth, and his horses' feed did not exceed coarse weeds. Wénzǐ heard of this and said, "One who can change after erring is a superior among the people." He was made a senior minister.
2.17 "Shūsūn Mùzǐ's Visit to Jìn"
Shūsūn Mùzǐ visited Jìn, and Duke Dào of Jìn hosted him with a banquet. The music reached the third repetition of "Lù Míng", and then he paid respects to the music three times. The Marquis of Jìn sent a messenger to inquire, saying, "You, sir, are using the ruler's command to pacify our exhausted state. You are using insufficient (i.e., humble) ceremonies for our late ruler to humiliate your attendants. You are using insufficient (i.e., humble) music to regulate it. My lord, you disregard the grand and bestow courtesy on the minor details. May I ask, what is the proper decorum?"
The envoy replied, "My humble ruler sent Bào to continue the goodwill of the late ruler. You, my lord, because of the relationship between feudal lords, bestowed great honors upon your envoy. Now, the music of the early music performance, the bronze instruments playing "Sì Xià Fán," "È," and "Qú," are what the Son of Heaven uses to entertain the first rank of feudal lords. The songs "Wén Wáng," "Dà Míng," and "Mián," are the music for when two rulers meet each other. All of these demonstrate luminous virtue to establish good relations. All of these are things your envoy would not dare to hear. Your servant thought it was merely practice and had no meaning so therefore I did not dare to bow. Now, the musicians singing songs and the three sections of the "Lù Míng," that the lord has bestowed upon his envoy, how dare your envoy not bow in gratitude for this bounty? Now, the "Lù Míng" is how the ruler praises the virtues of his predecessors. How dare I not respectfully accept this praise? "Sì Mǔ" is how the ruler commends the diligence of his envoys. How dare I not respectfully accept this commendation? In "Huáng Huáng Zhě Huá," the ruler instructs his envoys, saying, "Always be mindful of your inadequacy." Planning, strategizing, measuring, and inquiring, you must consult with Zhōu. How dare I not respectfully accept this instruction? I have heard it said: "Harmony is what it means to always be mindful," "Consulting about talent is what it means to plan (zōu)," "Consulting about affairs is what it means to strategize (móu)," "Consulting about righteousness is what it means to measure (dù)," "Consulting with relatives is what it means to inquire (xún)," "Loyalty and trustworthiness are what it means by Zhōu." The ruler bestows upon his envoys great courtesy, emphasizing it with the six virtues. How dare I not reverently return this great courtesy?"
2.18 Shū Sūn Mùzi Advises Jì Wǔzi Against Raising Three Armies
When Jì Wǔzi intended to raise three armies, Shū Sūn Mùzi said: “That is not permissible. The Son of Heaven makes the army, the dukes command it to punish those without virtue. The chief marquises make the army, the ministers command it to serve the Son of Heaven. The feudal lords have ministers but no army, they command the teachers and guards to assist the chief marquises. From counts, viscounts, and barons, they have grand officers but no ministers, they command the tax levies to follow the feudal lords. Therefore, those above can command those below, and those below have no treachery or evil. Now, I am a small marquis, situated between great states, diligently preparing tributes and levies to follow those we serve, yet still fearful of being punished. If we act as a chief marquis, angering the great states, would that not be impermissible?” He did not listen. He then created a central army. From this point on, Qí and Chǔ alternately attacked Lǔ, and Xiāng and Zhāo all went to Chǔ.
2.19 *Zhūhóu Fá Qín Lǔ Rén Yǐ Jǔ Rén Xiān Jì* (The feudal lords attack Qín, and the men of Lǔ have the men of Jǔ cross the river first).
The feudal lords attacked Qín. Jìn's Shū Xiàng saw Shūsūn Mùzǐ and said, "The feudal lords said that Qín was disrespectful and attacked them, but they stopped at the Jīng River. What benefit is that to Qín?" They reached the Jīng River, but could not cross. Mùzǐ said, "Bào's knowledge is in 'Páo Yǒu Kǔ Yè' [The Bitter Gourd Has Leaves], I don't know anything else." Shū Xiàng withdrew, summoned the Boat Officer and the Sīmǎ (Military Officer), and said, "The bitter gourd is not useful to people, only for crossing together. When Lǔ's Shūsūn recited 'Páo Yǒu Kǔ Yè', he must have intended to cross the river. Prepare the boats and clear the tunnels, and do not use shared methods." On this trip, the people of Lǔ let the people of Jǔ cross first, and the feudal lords followed them.
2.20 "Duke Xiāng's Visit to Chǔ"
Duke Xiāng went to Chǔ. When he reached the Hàn River, he heard that King Kāng had died and wanted to return. Shūzhòng Zhāo Bó said: "Your coming was not for the sake of one person, but for the sake of his name and his followers. Now the king is dead, his name has not yet been changed, and his followers have not yet been defeated. Why return?" All the senior officials wanted to return. Zǐfú Huì Bó said: "Not knowing what to do, let us temporarily follow the lord!" Shūzhòng said: "Your coming was not to secure your own safety, but for the benefit of the state. Therefore, you did not fear hardship and distance and listened to Chǔ; it was not to be righteous to Chǔ, but to fear its name and its followers. Those who are righteous certainly celebrate their joy and mourn their sorrow, how much more so to fear and submit to them? ( Having heard), you went out of fear, and having heard of the mourning, you return. If the Mǐ surname truly has an heir, who will take over the responsibility of the mourning? Moreover, the king's heir is already grown; the government has not changed. I came for the sake of my late lord, and to die and leave him would mean, who would say I am not as good as my late lord? To be about to hold the funeral rites, but to hear of the funeral and return, who would say that is not an insult? To serve one's lord and be entrusted with his government, who would doubt my loyalty? To seek to explain away the insult, and hurry to the former men, would that not only increase the enmity? Explaining away the insult is not cowardice, upholding the government is not disloyal, leading a great enemy to intimidate a small state, who would say that he is waiting for it? If following the lord means fleeing disaster, then it is better to disobey the lord to avoid hardship. Moreover, a jūnzǐ (君子) acts only after his plans are complete, have you gentlemen planned? If you have a strategy to resist Chǔ (楚) and preparations to defend the state, then you may stay; if you do not have them, it is better to go." Thereupon he departed.
Returning, reaching Fāngchéng (方城), he heard that Jì Wǔzǐ (季武子) attacked Biàn (卞). The duke wanted to return, and sent the Chu army to attack Lu. Róngchéng Bó said: "That won't do. The relationship between a ruler and his subjects should be one where the ruler's authority is great. If you cannot command your own state and rely on the feudal lords, who among the feudal lords will be close to you? If you obtain the Chu army to attack Lu, and since Lu has not violated its previous agreement to cede Biàn, they will certainly follow orders, and their defense will be strong. If Chu conquers Lu, the various Jī clans will not be able to spy on it, let alone you? Will they not perhaps place their own kind to subdue the Eastern Barbarians, and greatly expand the Xia territories, aiming to rule the world, and what benefit will that be to you, what will they give you? If they do not conquer Lu, and you attack it using barbarian tribes, and then seek to enter it again, you certainly will not succeed. It is better to grant it to him. In the past, Sù served you, and dared not fail to correct himself. Being drunk and angry, becoming sober and happy, what harm is there in mediocrity? Your Excellency, please enter!" Then he returned.
2.21 "Jì Yě Presents His Salary"
When Xiāng Gōng was in Chǔ, Jì Wǔzǐ took Biàn, and sent Jì Yě to meet him. He chased after him and gave him a sealed letter, saying, "The people of Biàn were about to rebel; your servant punished them and has already taken it." The Duke did not speak. Róngchéng Zǐ said, "You are the arms and legs of the state of Lǔ, the affairs of the state, you truly control them. Whatever you deem advantageous, why is Biàn necessary? If Biàn is guilty and you punish them, they are your subordinates, so what need is there to report it?" Jì Yě returned, presented his salary and did not serve, saying, He said: "To make me deceive my lord, is to say I am capable. If capable but deceiving one's lord, dare one enjoy his emolument and stand in his court?"
2.22 *Shūsūn Mùzǐ* Knows that *Chǔ*’s Crown Prince *Wéi* Has the Intention to Usurp the State
At the meeting at *Guó*, *Chǔ*'s Crown Prince *Wéi*, two men held halberds in front. *Cài*’s *Gōngsūn Guīshēng* and *Zhèng*’s *Hǎnhǔ* met with *Shūsūn Mùzǐ*. *Mùzǐ* said: "The *Chǔ* Crown Prince is very handsome, he will not just be a senior official, but a ruler." *Zhèng*’s *Zǐpí* said: "With those who hold halberds in front, I am confused by it." *Cài*’s *Zǐjiā* said: "*Chǔ* is a great state, and Crown Prince *Wéi* is its prime minister. To have those who hold halberds in front, is that not permissible?" *Mùzǐ* said: "It is not so. The Son of Heaven has tiger-braves, for military exercises; the feudal lords have chosen braves, to defend against disasters; high officials have two chariots, to prepare for service; knights have an accompanying rider, to announce messages and run errands. Now a high official displaying the attire of a feudal lord, he has the intention to usurp. If he does not have that intention, how dare he display that attire to meet the high officials of the feudal lords? He will not be admitted. Attire is, the outward expression of the heart, like a tortoise, when you burn its inside, the markings must appear on the outside. If the son of Chǔ does not become ruler, he will surely die, and not unite the feudal lords." Gōngzǐ Wéi rebelled, killing Jiá Áo and replacing him.
2.23 Shūsūn Mùzǐ Did Not Use Wealth to Privately Avoid Punishment
At the meeting of Guó, the high officials of the feudal lords, following their alliances, had not yet withdrawn. Jì Wǔzǐ 季武子 attacked Jǔ 莒 and took Yùn 鄆. The people of Jǔ 莒 complained to the alliance. The people of Chǔ 楚 were going to execute Shū Sūn Mùzǐ 叔孫穆子. Lè Wángfù 樂王鮒 of Jìn 晉 sought bribes from Mùzǐ 穆子, saying: "I will plead on your behalf to Chǔ 楚." Mùzǐ 穆子 did not give it to him. Liáng Qí Jìng 梁其踁 said to Mùzǐ 穆子: "Having wealth is to protect oneself. If offering wealth can achieve exemption, why do you begrudge it?" Mùzǐ 穆子 said: "This is not something you understand. I received the ruler's mandate to attend to important matters at the alliance, and the state is guilty of a crime. If I privately exempt myself with wealth, it means I am attending to my private affairs at the alliance. If it is acceptable to do that, then could one offer wealth to fulfill private desires? Even if I could be exempted, what about the matters of the feudal lords? Surely someone will follow my example, saying: 'There was a minister of a feudal lord who did such a thing; it is acceptable.' Then I would be seeking personal safety and setting a precedent for the feudal lords. This is what a gentleman worries about causing. To act without sincerity, someone will surely speak of it. This is to expose one's lack of sincerity. It is not that I cherish possessions, but that I detest insincerity. Moreover, the offense did not originate with me, so what harm is there in being executed?" The Chǔ 楚 people then pardoned him.
Mùzǐ 穆子 returned. Wǔzǐ 武子 went to comfort him, but he did not come out until noon. The person said: "You may come out now." Mùzǐ 穆子 said: "I do not shrink from being executed, but I am preserving my pillar. If the pillar breaks and the rafters collapse, I fear being crushed by them. Therefore, it is said that though one dies outside, to protect the clan within, is permissible. Now that I have escaped great shame, and yet cannot endure petty resentment, can I be considered capable?" Then he came out to see him.
2.24 《Zǐfú Huìbó cóng Jì Píngzǐ rú Jìn》 子服惠伯從季平子如晉 (Zǐfú Huìbó Follows Jì Píngzǐ to Jìn)
At the meeting in Píngqiū, Duke Zhāo of Jìn sent Shū Xiàng to decline on behalf of Duke Zhāo, not participating in the alliance. Zǐfú Huìbó said: "Jìn trusts the Mán and Yí tribes and abandons its brothers; its government must be of two minds. A divided heart will surely lose the feudal lords. How can it be only Lǔ? Those who lose their government will surely be a source of bitterness to others. Lǔ fears it will befall them, so we must be respectful. We must send a high minister to follow." Jì Píngzǐ said: "Then you mean me! If I go, Jìn will surely worry about me. Who will be of two minds for them?" Zǐfú Huìbó said: "Jiāo has already spoken of it. How dare I evade the difficulty? Jiāo requests to follow."
The people of Jìn arrested Píngzǐ. Zǐfú Huìbó met with Hán Xuānzǐ and said: "An alliance Trust is essential. Jìn 晉, as the leader of the alliance, should prioritize trust. If you form an alliance but abandon the Marquis of Lǔ 魯, then trust will certainly be lacking. Formerly, during the rebellion of the Luán 欒 clan, the people of Qí 齊 took advantage of the chaos in Jìn 晉 and attacked and seized Zhāogē 朝歌. Our former ruler, Duke Xiāng of Lǔ 魯襄公, dared not rest at ease. He dispatched Shū Sūn Bào 叔孫豹 to lead our humble forces. Crippled and lame, all set out, without anyone staying behind; all followed the officers, camped at Yōng Yú 雍渝, and together with Hán Dān Shèng 邯鄲勝 attacked the left flank of Qí 齊. We checked and stopped Yàn Lái 晏萊. Only after the Qí 齊 army retreated did we dare return. This was not because we sought to distance ourselves [from Qí 齊], but because Lǔ 魯 was so close to Qí 齊, and was also a small state. If Qí 齊 set out in the morning, they could reach the borders of Lǔ 魯 in the evening. We did not dare to fear its troubles, but shared its worries with Jìn 晉. We also said, "Perhaps we can be of some benefit to Lǔ 魯!" Now you trust the barbarians and abandon us. Now, if the feudal lords strive for the sake of their ruler, where will encouragement then rest? If you abandon Lǔ and merely secure the other feudal lords, would the assembled ministers dare to shrink from punishment? Among the feudal lords who serve Jìn, Lǔ strives the most. If you abandon them for the sake of barbarians and foreigners, would you not gain barbarians and foreigners while losing the trust of the feudal lords? If you calculate what is advantageous in this, the small states will share their fate." Xuānzi was pleased and then returned to report to Píngzi.
2.25 "Jì Huánzi Finds a Sheep While Digging a Well"
Jì Huánzi was digging a well and found something like an earthen jar, and within it was a sheep. He sent someone to ask Zhòngní, saying: "I dug a well and found a dog, what is this?" He replied: "According to what I, Qiū, have heard, it is a sheep. I, Qiū, have heard that: The strange things of wood and stone are called Kuí and Wǎngliǎng, the strange creatures of the water are called dragons (lóng) and wǎngxiàng; the strange creatures of the earth are called fén yáng."
2.26 *Gōngfǔ Wénbó zhī Mǔ Duì Jì Kāngzǐ Wèn*
Jì Kāngzǐ asked the mother of Gōngfǔ Wénbó, saying: "The mistress must have something to tell Féi." She replied: "I am only capable of growing old; how can I tell you anything?" Kāngzǐ said: "Even so, Féi wishes to hear something from you." She replied: "I heard from my late mother-in-law, 'If a gentleman is capable of labor, his descendants will continue.'" Zǐxià heard this and said: "Excellent! I (Shāng) have heard that 'In ancient times, those who married and did not have contact with their uncle-in-law or aunt-in-law were considered unfortunate.' A married couple learning from their uncle-in-law and aunt-in-law *lǐ yě.* ("This is proper etiquette.")
2.27 *Gōngfǔ Wénbó Yǐn Nángōng Jìngshū Jiǔ* ("Gōngfǔ Wénbó Gives Nángōng Jìngshū Wine")
*Gōngfǔ Wénbó* gave *Nángōng Jìngshū* wine, with *Lù Dǔfǔ* as a guest. The turtle offered was small. *Dǔfǔ* was angry, They invited each other to eat the turtle, but he declined, saying: "I will wait until the turtle is bigger before eating it." He then left. *Wénbó*'s mother heard of this, and angrily said: "I heard from my late husband that: 'Sacrifices nourish the deceased, banquets nourish honored guests.' What fault is there in the turtle? That you would make the noble guest angry!" She then expelled him. After five days, the wife of the ruler of *Lǔ* interceded, and he was reinstated.
2.28 *Gōngfǔ Wénbó zhī Mǔ Lùn Nèi Cháo Yǔ Wài Cháo* ("Gōngfǔ Wénbó's Mother Discusses the Inner and Outer Courts")
